period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 7 periods = 280 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

periods.activity_title: First Encounter: Road Safety Letter Read-Aloud

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the chapter by asking children where they have seen traffic police and what those officers do. A brief elicitation primes attention for the letter format that follows.

Teacher reads the full letter from traffic officer Bharat aloud (Textbook pp.25–27), pointing to each numbered rule illustration as it is read. Tone is warm and direct, mirroring the letter's register.
Shared reading: children follow in their books as teacher re-reads the six rules together, pausing after each rule so students repeat the key instruction aloud as a class.
Quick oral recap — teacher asks children to name as many of the six rules as they can from memory, accepting any order. Responses are acknowledged but not corrected in writing yet.

periods.teacher_notes: The chapter is structured as a friendly letter, which is unusual for an informational text — draw attention to the greeting and sign-off so children notice the genre cue. Each rule has an accompanying illustration; pausing at each one helps children connect the visual to the instruction.

periods.activity_title: Comprehension Discussion: Thinking About the Rules

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — A. (p.28): answer three questions about road-safety rules in full sentences.
Let us Think — B. (p.28): decide true or false for six statements about pedestrian safety.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays the six rules on the board as a numbered list (written from memory with class help) to warm up reading of the letter text on pp.25–27.
Let us Think — A. (p.28): teacher reads each question aloud, then students discuss in pairs before one pair shares aloud. Teacher models a complete-sentence answer for the first question.
Let us Think — B. (p.28): teacher reads each statement; students hold up a thumb-up or thumb-down card, then justify their verdict by pointing to the relevant rule in the text.
Whole-class debrief — teacher invites one student to summarise in one sentence what officer Bharat wants children to remember most.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often confuse Rule 1 (look right-left-right) with simply 'looking both ways' — nudge them to name the sequence precisely when answering question 1. The true/false statements include one about reflective stickers and dark clothes (statement 4, which is false) that children frequently get wrong; pause to reread Rule 5 together before judging it.

periods.activity_title: Speaking About Road Safety: Guided Conversation

time_bands.activity: Teacher recaps the six road-safety rules from the letter by pointing to illustrations on pp.25–27 and asking children which rule each picture shows. This activates the content for speaking.

Guided conversation — teacher poses situational prompts one at a time: 'You are at a busy road with no adult. What do you do?' and 'Your friend wants to play near the road. What would you say?' Students respond in full spoken sentences, referring to the rules.

Role-play in pairs: one child is a pedestrian about to cross unsafely; the other is a traffic officer who stops them and explains the correct rule. Teacher circulates, prompting use of the words 'pedestrian', 'footpath', and 'zebra crossing' from the New Words box.
A few pairs share their role-play with the class. Teacher acknowledges accurate rule references and correct use of chapter vocabulary.

periods.teacher_notes: Children at this stage often revert to listing rules rather than speaking in conversational sentences — model the difference between 'Rule 3: footpath' and a full spoken response before the pair work. The New Words box (pp.25–27) introduces 'pedestrian', 'footpath', 'reflective', and 'distract'; encourage these during role-play rather than correcting after.

periods.activity_title: Writing Workshop: Safe and Unsafe Activities and a Thank-You Letter

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — A. (p.30): classify five activities as safe or unsafe with a written label.
Let us Write — D. (p.30–31): write a thank-you letter to officer Bharat using the provided starter.

time_bands.activity: Let us Write — A. (p.30): teacher reads each of the five activities aloud. Students write 'Safe' or 'Unsafe' beside each one in their books, then share answers with a partner. Teacher quickly confirms correct answers as a class.

Modelled writing — teacher writes the opening of the thank-you letter on the board using the starter from Let us Write — D. (p.30–31): 'Dear Traffic Police Officer…', thinking aloud about which two or three rules from the letter to mention in the response.

Students write their own letter in full, completing the starter on p.30–31. Teacher circulates, nudging children to name at least one specific rule they promise to follow and to use the words 'pedestrian' or 'footpath' at least once.

Two or three students read their letters aloud. Class listens and gives a thumbs-up when they hear a specific road-safety rule mentioned. Teacher offers brief formative feedback on letter conventions (greeting, sign-off, name).

periods.teacher_notes: The letter starter on p.30–31 provides the opening but children must complete '…I have read your letter carefully and understood that…' — encourage them to write at least two complete sentences from this point, naming specific rules rather than restating them vaguely. Watch for children who write only one word ('safe') after the starter; prompt with 'What have you understood about the zebra crossing?'

periods.activity_title: Grammar in Context: Countable and Uncountable Nouns

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — A. (p.32): classify fourteen food items as countable (C) or uncountable (U).
Let us Learn — B. (p.33): classify eleven road-and-transport words as countable or uncountable.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces countable and uncountable nouns using the grammar box on p.32, contrasting 'apples' (can be counted) with 'water' (cannot). Children give two examples each of countable and uncountable things they see in class.

Let us Learn — A. (p.32): teacher reads each word in the list aloud. Students write 'C' or 'U' in their books. After every four items, the class compares answers and teacher explains any disagreements using a real-world test ('Can you say one banana? Yes — countable.').

Let us Learn — B. (p.33): the word list now uses road and transport vocabulary from the chapter — traffic, helmet, speed, pedestrian, safety, fuel, etc. Students complete the table individually, then pairs compare. Teacher highlights how the same concept applies whether the words are food or road-safety terms.
Quick oral word-game: teacher calls a word at random from either task list; students call back 'countable!' or 'uncountable!' as fast as they can, keeping it as a whole-class chant.

periods.teacher_notes: The trickiest items in Task A are those where the same substance can be both depending on form — 'coffee' (uncountable) versus 'coffee jars' (countable) on p.32. Use this contrast explicitly to show children that packaging or container transforms the noun. Task B is directly connected to the chapter's road-safety vocabulary, which helps children see grammar in context rather than in isolation.

periods.activity_title: Word Work: Countable and Uncountable Nouns in a Recipe

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — C. (p.33): underline countable and circle uncountable nouns in the banana milkshake recipe.

homework.task_brief: Let us Think — C. (pp.28–29): choose the correct option for three road-safety questions and write the answer in your exercise book.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the banana milkshake recipe on p.33 aloud once at a natural pace while children follow in their books. Teacher then asks: 'Which ingredients can you count one by one?' to prime the identification task.

Let us Learn — C. (p.33): students work individually, underlining countable nouns (bananas, glass, ice cubes) and circling uncountable nouns (milk, sugar, honey) in the recipe. Teacher circulates and prompts with questions like 'Can you say one sugar? Try it — does it sound right?'

Whole-class checking: teacher writes the recipe on the board step by step, calling on students to say which words to underline and which to circle, and to state the reason for each choice in one spoken sentence.

Brief contextual-prediction wrap-up: teacher says a new phrase (e.g. 'a jar of honey', 'three apples') and children decide whether the noun inside is countable or uncountable, explaining why in a spoken sentence.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked through food-item and road-safety word lists in the earlier grammar unit, children are now expected to apply the same distinction independently to a running recipe text — the shift from a list to continuous prose is the new challenge here. Watch for children who circle 'bananas' as uncountable; point back to the 'two bananas' phrase in Step 1 of the recipe as the evidence.

periods.activity_title: Beyond the Text: Spot the Road-Safety Errors

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do — B. (p.31): study the busy road picture and identify six road-safety errors in writing.

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites children to recall the six road-safety rules from officer Bharat's letter on pp.25–27 by asking: 'What would a perfectly safe road scene look like?' Children suggest details aloud while teacher lists key features on the board.

Teacher directs children to the picture on p.31 (Let us Do — B.) and asks them to study it quietly, looking for anything that contradicts the safe road scene they just described. Children work individually and note down errors as they spot them.

Pair discussion: partners compare their lists and agree on the six errors. Teacher circulates, prompting children to connect each error to its specific rule from the letter ('Which rule does this break?').

Whole-class share-out: pairs call out one error each in turn. Teacher writes confirmed errors on the board, linking each to the rule it violates. Children check and complete any they missed in their own books.

periods.teacher_notes: The picture on p.31 contains six deliberate errors — the most commonly missed are the reflective-sticker absence in the evening scene and the person using headphones near traffic. Prompt pairs who have only four errors to look again at the traffic-light colour and the pedestrian's hand-holding. Unanchored task: Let us Do — A. (p.31, safe/unsafe activity classification) was covered in the writing unit and does not need re-teaching here; students may revisit it independently.

items.source_context: Six numbered pedestrian road-safety rules in a letter from traffic officer Bharat.
items.item_stem: Traffic officer Bharat gives six road-safety rules in his letter. Which rule tells pedestrians where exactly to walk near a busy road?

options.label: A
options.text: Always hold an adult's hand while crossing.

options.label: B
options.text: Stick reflective stickers on your clothes in the evening.

options.label: C
options.text: Wait for the pedestrian green signal before crossing.

options.label: D
options.text: Walk on the footpath, away from moving vehicles.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may be conflating Rule 4 (hold an adult's hand) with Rule 3 (walk on footpath).
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student may be recalling Rule 5 (reflective stickers) without connecting it to the question about where to walk.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student may be thinking of Rule 2 (traffic lights) and mixing up different safety rules.

items.item_stem: In his letter, officer Bharat explains why children should avoid using headphones or mobile phones near traffic. In your own words, explain what danger he warns about and name one other distraction he mentions.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Officer Bharat warns that headphones and mobile phones can distract you so you cannot hear traffic sounds, which may cause an accident. He also mentions playing near the road as another dangerous distraction.

items.source_context: Role-play and guided conversation about pedestrian rules from officer Bharat's letter.
items.item_stem: Listen carefully. Your teacher will describe a situation: 'A child is about to cross a busy road. There is no adult nearby, the traffic light shows red for vehicles, and there is a zebra crossing a little further ahead.' Which of the following describes what the child should do, according to officer Bharat's letter?

options.text: The child should cross immediately because the road is clear.
The child should run quickly across the road while the vehicles are stopped at the red light.
The child should wait at the crossing and use the pedestrian green signal before crossing.
The child should walk to the zebra crossing, look right, left, and right again, and cross only when safe.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 follows Rule 1 (use the zebra crossing, look right-left-right). Statement 3 follows Rule 2 (wait for the pedestrian green signal). Statements 1 and 4 are false because running or crossing without checking signals violates Rules 1 and 2.

items.item_stem: Imagine you are officer Bharat. Your friend is about to cross the road while listening to loud music on headphones. Speak aloud: tell your friend which rule they are breaking and what they should do instead. Use the words 'distract' and 'footpath' in your answer.

expected_elements: Names Rule 6: headphones distract from traffic sounds.
Tells friend to remove headphones and stay alert.

items.item_stem: Match each road-safety error with the rule from officer Bharat's letter that it breaks.
items.visual_stimulus:
Error Spotted | Rule Broken
A child crossing without looking right-left-right | Rule 1: Always use the zebra crossing
A pedestrian walking on the road instead of the pavement | Rule 3: Walk on the footpath
A child crossing while the pedestrian signal is red | Rule 2: Follow the traffic lights
A person wearing headphones near moving vehicles | Rule 6: Be alert

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Row 1 — Rule 1; Row 2 — Rule 3; Row 3 — Rule 2; Row 4 — Rule 6.

answer_key.left: A child crossing without looking right-left-right
answer_key.right: Rule 1: Always use the zebra crossing

answer_key.left: A pedestrian walking on the road instead of the pavement
